# Pharmacotherapy for Obesity

## Historical Context and FDA-Approved Agents

The pharmacological treatment of obesity has been marked by cycles of optimism and retrenchment, punctuated by the withdrawal of agents whose cardiovascular or neuropsychiatric risks outweighed their benefits. Amphetamine derivatives dominated the mid-twentieth century, followed by fenfluramine and phentermine combinations, which were withdrawn in 1997 after reports of valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension. The endocannabinoid receptor antagonist rimonabant, approved in Europe in 2006, was withdrawn globally by 2008 following evidence of severe neuropsychiatric adverse events, including suicidality, that emerged in post-marketing surveillance. Similarly, the norepinephrine–serotonin reuptake inhibitor sibutramine was voluntarily withdrawn from the market in 2010 after the Sibutramine Cardiovascular OUTcomes (SCOUT) trial, which enrolled 10,742 high-risk patients, demonstrated a significant increase in the composite risk of nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke compared with placebo, compelling regulatory agencies in both the United States and Europe to mandate its removal [@Yanovski2014Longterm]. These withdrawals fundamentally reshaped the regulatory framework for anti-obesity medications, with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration now requiring dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trials for new agents, and they reinforced the primacy of safety alongside efficacy in drug development.

As of 2024, six pharmacological agents or combinations hold FDA approval for chronic weight management in adults with obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²) or overweight (BMI ≥ 27 kg/m²) with at least one weight-related comorbidity: orlistat (Xenical/Alli), phentermine/topiramate extended-release (Qsymia), naltrexone/bupropion extended-release (Contrave), liraglutide 3.0 mg subcutaneous daily (Saxenda), semaglutide 2.4 mg subcutaneous weekly (Wegovy), and tirzepatide 5–15 mg subcutaneous weekly (Zepbound, approved in November 2023). Clinical practice guidelines from the Endocrine Society and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists provide structured decision frameworks for agent selection based on comorbidities, contraindications, and patient preference [@Apovian2015Pharmacological; @Garvey2016American]. The magnitude of weight loss achievable with pharmacotherapy has increased dramatically with each successive generation of agents, from a mean excess of approximately 3–4 kg with orlistat to more than 20% total body weight with tirzepatide, a progression that reflects deepening mechanistic understanding of the central and peripheral regulators of energy homeostasis.

## Older Anti-Obesity Medications

Orlistat (Xenical) 120 mg administered three times daily with meals acts as a reversible inhibitor of gastric and pancreatic lipases, reducing the absorption of dietary fat by approximately 30%. The landmark XENical in the Prevention of Diabetes in Obese Subjects (XENDOS) trial, conducted by @Torgerson2004Xenical and enrolling 3,305 obese Swedish adults with either normal glucose tolerance or impaired glucose tolerance, demonstrated over four years that orlistat in conjunction with lifestyle modification produced a 37% relative risk reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes compared with placebo (6.2% versus 9.0%, p = 0.0032), alongside a modest 2.8 kg incremental weight loss advantage. The gastrointestinal tolerability profile of orlistat, characterized by oily spotting, fecal urgency, flatus with discharge, and fecal incontinence in up to 20–27% of users during the first year, substantially limits long-term adherence and renders it poorly suited for patients requiring consistent employment-related or social functioning. Nevertheless, its lack of systemic absorption and absence of cardiovascular or neuropsychiatric risk signals distinguish orlistat as an option for patients in whom other agents are contraindicated.

The combination of phentermine and topiramate extended-release (Qsymia) exploits complementary mechanisms: phentermine releases catecholamines in the hypothalamus to suppress appetite, while topiramate augments gamma-aminobutyric acid activity and inhibits carbonic anhydrase, contributing to satiety and modest glucose-lowering. The pivotal CONQUER trial, reported by @Gadde2011Effects and enrolling 2,487 overweight or obese adults with two or more weight-related comorbidities, demonstrated dose-dependent weight loss of 7.8% of baseline body weight with the recommended 7.5 mg/46 mg dose and 9.8% with the high dose (15 mg/92 mg), compared with 1.2% with placebo, at 56 weeks (p < 0.001 for both active doses). Beyond weight reduction, the CONQUER cohort exhibited clinically meaningful improvements in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, waist circumference, and fasting glucose. However, teratogenicity attributable to topiramate, which carries a risk of oral cleft in first-trimester fetal exposure approximately five-fold higher than background rates, necessitates a mandatory risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program, monthly pregnancy testing in women of childbearing potential, and robust contraception counseling, representing a significant barrier to broad prescription in premenopausal women.

The fixed-dose combination of naltrexone 32 mg and bupropion 360 mg extended-release (Contrave) operates by engaging the hypothalamic melanocortin system: bupropion activates pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in the arcuate nucleus, increasing alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone and thereby suppressing appetite, while naltrexone blocks mu-opioid receptor–mediated autoinhibitory feedback on POMC neurons, sustaining and amplifying this anorectic signal. The Contrave Obesity Research I (COR-I) trial, conducted by @Greenway2010Effect in 1,453 overweight and obese adults, demonstrated 6.1% weight loss with naltrexone/bupropion versus 1.3% with placebo at 56 weeks (p < 0.001), with 42% of active-treatment participants achieving at least 5% weight loss compared with 17% on placebo. The combination carries a boxed warning regarding neuropsychiatric adverse events and suicidal ideation consistent with bupropion labeling, is contraindicated in patients receiving opioid analgesics or undergoing opioid withdrawal, and requires cardiovascular monitoring given transient blood pressure elevations observed early in treatment.

## GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

The discovery and pharmacological exploitation of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) represents perhaps the most consequential advance in obesity therapeutics since the turn of the millennium. GLP-1, secreted by intestinal L-cells in response to nutrient ingestion, acts on GLP-1 receptors (GLP-1R) distributed throughout the central nervous system, particularly within the arcuate nucleus and nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) of the hypothalamus, as well as on vagal afferent neurons projecting from the gastrointestinal tract [@Drucker2018Mechanisms; @Holst2007Physiology]. Receptor activation in these regions suppresses appetite, promotes satiety signaling, and reduces the hedonic drive to eat, while peripheral GLP-1R signaling in the pancreatic beta cell augments glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decelerates gastric emptying, and modulates hepatic glucose output. The overall metabolic consequence is a coordinated reduction in caloric intake and improvement in glycaemic homeostasis that extends well beyond the simple glucose-lowering effect that characterized earlier incretin therapeutics [@Muller2019Glucagon].

Liraglutide 3.0 mg, administered as a daily subcutaneous injection and approved by the FDA in 2014 under the brand name Saxenda, was evaluated in the pivotal SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial reported by @PiSunyer2015Randomized, which randomized 3,731 non-diabetic adults with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² or ≥ 27 kg/m² with dyslipidaemia or hypertension to liraglutide 3.0 mg or placebo, both with lifestyle counseling, for 56 weeks. The liraglutide group achieved a mean weight loss of 8.0% of baseline body weight compared with 2.6% in the placebo arm (p < 0.001), with 63.2% versus 27.1% achieving at least 5% weight loss and 33.1% versus 10.6% achieving at least 10% weight loss. Gastrointestinal adverse events were prominent, with nausea occurring in approximately 40% and vomiting in approximately 15% of liraglutide-treated participants, predominantly during the first eight weeks of dose escalation; these events led to discontinuation in approximately 10% of participants. Liraglutide at its lower cardiovascular dose of 1.8 mg also demonstrated a significant reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes patients in the LEADER trial [@Marso2016Liraglutide], providing mechanistic plausibility for cardiovascular benefit at the obesity dose.

Semaglutide 2.4 mg administered once weekly—a structural analogue of liraglutide engineered with an extended half-life enabling weekly rather than daily dosing and substantially greater receptor occupancy—transformed expectations for pharmacological weight management. The STEP 1 trial, reported by @Wilding2021Once and enrolling 1,961 adults without type 2 diabetes (mean body weight 105.4 kg, mean BMI 37.9 kg/m²), demonstrated a mean weight loss of 14.9% of body weight versus 2.4% with placebo at 68 weeks (difference −12.4 percentage points, p < 0.001), corresponding to an absolute mean loss of 15.3 kg. Proportional responders were striking: 86.4% of semaglutide participants achieved at least 5% weight loss compared with 31.5% on placebo, 69.1% versus 12.0% achieved at least 10%, and 50.5% versus 4.9% achieved at least 15% weight loss, figures that had previously been attainable only with bariatric surgery. In the STEP 2 trial among 1,210 adults with type 2 diabetes, @Davies2021Semaglutide demonstrated that while semaglutide 2.4 mg produced a mean weight loss of 9.6% versus 3.4% with placebo (p < 0.001), the presence of type 2 diabetes attenuated the weight loss response compared with the non-diabetic STEP 1 cohort—a finding consistent with impaired GLP-1 responsiveness in established insulin resistance. The STEP 3 trial, conducted by @Wadden2021Effect in 611 adults receiving semaglutide as an adjunct to an intensive behavioral intervention featuring a structured low-calorie dietary phase, demonstrated weight losses of 16.0% versus 5.7% in the placebo-plus-intensive-therapy group, underscoring the additive benefits of pharmacotherapy and structured behavioral support. A direct head-to-head comparison by @Rubino2021Effect confirmed the superiority of once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg over once-daily liraglutide 3.0 mg for body weight reduction, lending empirical support to prescribing prioritization of the newer agent.

A critical concern with all anti-obesity pharmacotherapies—and one with direct implications for treatment planning and healthcare economics—is weight regain after drug cessation. The STEP 1 extension study, reported by @Wilding2022Weight, followed 327 participants who had completed the initial 68-week trial through a further year off treatment. By one year after withdrawal, participants had regained approximately two-thirds of their prior weight loss, recovering a mean of 11.6 percentage points of the initial 17.3% reduction, with cardiometabolic risk markers returning toward baseline levels. This finding firmly establishes semaglutide, and by extension other incretin-based agents, as therapies that require indefinite continuation to maintain benefit—a consideration that profoundly affects cost-effectiveness modeling and patient counseling.

The cardiovascular benefit of semaglutide 2.4 mg was definitively established by the SELECT (Semaglutide Effects on Cardiovascular Outcomes in People with Overweight or Obesity) trial, reported by @Lincoff2023Semaglutide. This landmark event-driven outcomes trial enrolled 17,604 adults with established cardiovascular disease, overweight or obesity (BMI ≥ 27 kg/m²), but without diabetes, and followed them for a median of 3.3 years. Treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly produced a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke compared with placebo (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.72–0.90, p < 0.001), with a number needed to treat of approximately 67 over three years. Crucially, this cardiovascular benefit was independent of baseline HbA1c or the degree of weight loss achieved, suggesting direct cardioprotective effects of GLP-1R agonism beyond glucose or weight lowering, and establishing semaglutide as the first anti-obesity medication with proven mortality-reducing cardiovascular benefit in a predominantly non-diabetic population.

## Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonist: Tirzepatide

Tirzepatide represents a structural and mechanistic advance over pure GLP-1R agonists, functioning as a synthetic dual agonist at both the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) and GLP-1R. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), secreted by duodenal and jejunal K-cells, acts on GIPR in adipose tissue to regulate lipolysis and lipid storage, in the central nervous system to modulate energy balance, and in the pancreas to augment insulin secretion [@Holst2020GIP]. The GIP component of tirzepatide is thought to amplify adipose lipolysis, reduce ectopic lipid deposition, and potentiate the anorectic signaling of GLP-1R co-activation through synergistic hypothalamic effects, yielding a degree of weight loss substantially greater than that achieved by selective GLP-1R agonism alone [@Muller2022Antiobesity].

The SURMOUNT-1 trial, reported by @Jastreboff2022Tirzepatide and enrolling 2,539 adults without type 2 diabetes (mean body weight 104.8 kg), demonstrated dose-dependent weight loss at 72 weeks: 15.0% with tirzepatide 5 mg, 19.5% with 10 mg, and 20.9% with 15 mg, compared with 3.1% in the placebo group (p < 0.001 for all doses). Among participants receiving the 15 mg dose, 91.1% achieved at least 5% weight loss, 82.8% achieved at least 10%, 62.4% achieved at least 15%, and 57.9% achieved at least 20% weight loss—the latter a threshold previously considered exclusive to surgical intervention. Nausea was reported by 39.4% of participants in the 15 mg group, consistent with incretin-class effects, and was predominantly mild to moderate in severity and transient, concentrated in the dose-escalation period. The SURMOUNT-2 trial, conducted by @Garvey2023Tirzepatide in 938 adults with type 2 diabetes, demonstrated weight losses of 12.8%, 14.7%, and 15.7% with tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg, and 15 mg respectively, versus 3.3% with placebo (p < 0.001 for all comparisons), with greater efficacy than comparably studied semaglutide doses in the type 2 diabetes population.

The SURMOUNT-3 trial, reported by @Wadden2023Tirzepatide in 806 adults who underwent an intensive lifestyle lead-in program for 12 weeks before randomization, demonstrated that tirzepatide initiated after behavioral optimization produced a further 18.4% weight reduction from randomization (on top of an initial lifestyle-induced 6.9% loss during lead-in), versus 2.5% with placebo following the same lead-in, yielding a combined total body weight loss of approximately 24% from initial screening weight. This sequential approach—behavioral optimization followed by pharmacotherapy—may represent an optimized real-world treatment paradigm. The durability of tirzepatide's weight-loss effect was examined in the SURMOUNT-4 maintenance trial, reported by @Aronne2024Continued, in which 670 participants who had completed 36 weeks of open-label tirzepatide (achieving a mean 20.9% weight loss) were randomized to continue tirzepatide or switch to placebo for a further 52 weeks. Those continuing tirzepatide achieved an additional 5.5% weight reduction, while those switched to placebo regained 14.0% of body weight; absolute weight change from randomization was −3.4 kg versus +11.2 kg (p < 0.001), again confirming the requirement for ongoing treatment to maintain benefit.

Beyond primary obesity management, tirzepatide demonstrated potent efficacy for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in the SURMOUNT-NASH trial reported by @Loomba2024Tirzepatide, which randomized 190 adults with biopsy-proven MASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis (stage F2 or F3). MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis was achieved in 62.4% of participants on tirzepatide 10 mg and 79.1% on 15 mg, compared with 9.7% on placebo; fibrosis improvement by at least one stage was observed in 35.4% and 44.9% of the 10 mg and 15 mg groups respectively, versus 14.9% for placebo (p < 0.001 for both), establishing tirzepatide as the most efficacious agent tested to date for MASH.

## Emerging Pharmacotherapy

The development pipeline for obesity pharmacotherapy has accelerated substantially, with several agents demonstrating unprecedented efficacy in phase 2 trials. Retatrutide, a first-in-class triple receptor agonist targeting GLP-1R, GIPR, and the glucagon receptor simultaneously, exploits the weight-reducing effects of GLP-1R and GIPR co-agonism while adding glucagon receptor stimulation to enhance energy expenditure via hepatic fatty acid oxidation and thermogenesis. In a phase 2 dose-ranging trial reported by @Jastreboff2023Triple enrolling 338 adults with obesity over 48 weeks, the 12 mg dose of retatrutide produced a mean body weight reduction of 24.2%—the largest weight loss observed with any pharmacological agent in a randomized controlled trial as of 2024—with 26.1% of participants in the highest-dose group achieving at least 30% weight loss. Among investigational amylin analogue combinations, cagrilintide, a long-acting amylin analogue, has been studied in combination with semaglutide (CagriSema) in phase 2 trials, with preliminary data suggesting weight losses of approximately 15–17% superior to either agent alone, though phase 3 confirmatory data were pending at the time of this review. Bimagrumab, a monoclonal antibody against the activin receptor IIA/IIB (ActRII), represents a mechanistically distinct approach: by inhibiting myostatin signalling, it preferentially reduces fat mass while preserving or increasing lean body mass, potentially addressing the muscle-sparing limitation common to caloric-restriction-based approaches. The broader pipeline, comprehensively reviewed by @Muller2022Antiobesity, also encompasses fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) analogues targeting hepatic and adipose metabolism, small-molecule PCSK9 inhibitors for concurrent lipid management, and mitochondrial uncouplers, collectively signalling a probable shift toward combination pharmacotherapy targeting multiple regulatory axes.

## Practical Considerations

Effective pharmacotherapy for obesity requires individualized shared decision-making that integrates clinical factors, patient preferences, cost, and insurance access. The adverse event profiles common to GLP-1R agonists and the dual GIP/GLP-1R agonist tirzepatide are largely consistent across the class: nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea occur in 40–50% of patients overall, are predominantly mild to moderate, and cluster in the initial four to sixteen weeks of dose titration, with incidence declining substantially after dose stabilization [@WilsonPetruk2023obesity]. Class-wide contraindications include a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, based on dose-dependent thyroid C-cell hyperplasia observed in rodent studies, although the clinical relevance in humans remains uncertain. Acute pancreatitis, while rare (estimated frequency approximately 0.2% in trial populations), represents a serious potential adverse event, and patients presenting with persistent severe abdominal pain during treatment should be evaluated promptly; the combination with alcohol, hypertriglyceridaemia, and cholelithiasis (itself associated with rapid weight loss) augments risk. The SELECT trial data for semaglutide and the anticipated results of the ongoing SURMOUNT-MMO cardiovascular outcomes trial for tirzepatide collectively position the incretin class as having not only metabolic but potentially cardiovascular disease-modifying properties that extend the benefit-risk analysis strongly in favor of treatment for high-risk patients [@Lincoff2023Semaglutide].

From a monitoring standpoint, clinical guidelines recommend baseline assessment including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, fasting lipids, and HbA1c before initiation, with repeat assessment at three and six months and annually thereafter [@Apovian2015Pharmacological]. Weight should be assessed at every clinical encounter during dose titration, typically every four weeks in the first six months. A practical threshold for response prediction—grounded in clinical trial responder analyses—is the achievement of at least 5% weight loss by twelve to sixteen weeks; patients who do not meet this threshold are unlikely to be meaningful long-term responders and merit reassessment of adherence, dose adequacy, or consideration of alternative agents or escalation to bariatric surgery. The emergence of medications achieving 15–25% total body weight loss has profoundly altered the treatment landscape by narrowing the efficacy gap between pharmacotherapy and surgery, while the confirmed cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide and the promising hepatic data for tirzepatide extend therapeutic applications well beyond anthropometric outcomes alone.
